stem: A 35-year-old patient presents with shortness of breath and chest pain. CT scan of the chest reveals a mediastinal mass containing fat and bone. The patient is otherwise stable and has no systemic symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
expl: Fat and bone in an anterior mediastinal mass = mature teratoma. Teratomas don't respond to chemo or radiotherapy → complete surgical resection (no biopsy needed with typical CT and normal markers).

why.D: Symptomatic and can grow, rupture or get infected.

stem: A patient underwent a CT scan for a mediastinal lesion. The CT showed a thin, fluid-filled structure next to the heart. What is most likely the diagnosis?
expl: A thin-walled, fluid-filled structure next to the heart (classically at the right cardiophrenic angle) = pericardial cyst.

why.A: Bronchogenic cysts lie next to the trachea/carina.
why.C: Oesophageal duplication cysts are posterior, next to the oesophagus.
why.D: Tamponade is fluid around the whole heart with haemodynamic compromise, not a cyst.

stem: A 26 year old male did a CT after trauma, it was clear but we found an incidental anterior mediastinal mass, he was asymptomatic and the mass showed calcifications, STM: b-HCG and AFP were elevated. Which of the following is the next step management for this patient?
expl: An anterior mediastinal mass with raised β-hCG and AFP in a young man = non-seminomatous germ cell tumour. Before calling it a primary mediastinal GCT, exclude a testicular primary → testicular ultrasound.

why.A: Raised AFP is diagnostic of NSGCT — biopsy isn't needed, and mediastinoscopy doesn't reach the anterior mediastinum.
why.C: PET is not routine for germ cell tumours.

stem: A 34 year old female did undergo a CT scan for chest pain. An anterior mediastinal mass was found, the mass showed calcifications as well as teeth and bones, STM: b-HCG and AFP were normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Calcification with teeth and bone and normal tumour markers in an anterior mediastinal mass = mature teratoma.

why.A: Seminoma is a homogeneous soft-tissue mass in young men.
why.B: NSGCT has raised AFP/β-hCG and is heterogeneous.
why.D: Thymoma doesn't contain teeth or bone.

stem: A 28-year-old male with a history of non-seminomatous germ cell tumor is currently undergoing chemotherapy. He presents with new-onset shortness of breath and chest pain. Follow-up imaging reveals a rapidly enlarging mediastinal mass despite normalization of serum tumor markers. What is the most likely diagnosis?

opts.t: Recurrent malignant germ cell tumor resistant to chehemotherapy

expl: During chemotherapy for NSGCT the malignant component dies (markers normalize) but the chemo-resistant teratoma keeps growing → growing teratoma syndrome. Stop chemotherapy and resect.

why.D: Resistant malignant tumour would raise the markers.

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with fever, severe chest pain, and neck swelling. He has a recent history of dental infection. CT scan shows air in the mediastinum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever, chest pain and neck swelling after a dental infection with mediastinal air = descending necrotizing mediastinitis (infection tracking down the retrovisceral space) → antibiotics + urgent drainage/debridement.

why.A: Pericarditis doesn't follow a dental infection with mediastinal gas.
why.B: Pneumothorax is air in the pleura.
why.D: Pneumonia doesn't cause neck swelling and mediastinal air.

stem: A stable patient has pneumomediastinum, and endoscopy shows a contained oesophageal leak (written in the source as "contained oesophageal bleeding"). What is the best management?
expl: A contained oesophageal leak in a stable patient is managed conservatively: NPO, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, PPI, nutrition and close observation; operate if it is uncontained or the patient becomes septic/unstable.
ansText: NPO and IV antibiotics — a contained, stable perforation is managed conservatively (NPO, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, PPI, nutrition, close observation). Operate if uncontained, septic or unstable.

stem: Coughed then had neck pain imaging showed pneumomediastinum?

opts.t: extension of air from the lung

srcNote: Abbreviated recall; only three choices are provided in the source.
expl: Most pneumomediastinum comes from alveolar rupture (e.g. coughing, asthma, vomiting) with air tracking along the bronchovascular sheaths to the mediastinum — not from tracheal or oesophageal injury.

why.A: Less common and follows major trauma or instrumentation.
why.C: Oesophageal injury follows vomiting (Boerhaave) or instrumentation and the patient is septic.

stem: A 36 year old woman with no significant past medical history admitted with symptoms of ptosis and diplopia. The patient has a positive tensilon test and the chest CT showed a 5 cm *6 cm homogenous mass in the anterior mediastinum. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Ptosis and diplopia with a positive Tensilon (edrophonium) test = myasthenia gravis; a homogeneous anterior mediastinal mass in that setting = thymoma.

why.A: Hodgkin lymphoma gives B symptoms and nodes, not myasthenia.
why.D: Teratoma is heterogeneous (fat, calcification) and unrelated to MG.

stem: 40 YO male patient presents with dysphagia and difficulty breathing. Investigations show an anterior mediastinal mass with negative serum markers, on imaging CT showed homogenous mass
srcNote: (Mediastinal pathology) Incomplete recall: the source omits an explicit question sentence and gives option D as "??".
expl: A homogeneous anterior mediastinal mass in a 40-year-old man with negative tumour markers fits a pure seminoma (treated with BEP chemotherapy).

why.B: NSGCT raises AFP/β-hCG and is heterogeneous.
why.C: Lymphoma is possible, but the key chose seminoma (LDH may be raised in both; lymphoma usually brings B symptoms and nodes elsewhere).

stem: 18 year old male, receiving chemotherapy for an anterior mediastinal mass, he developed worsening SOB after his second chemo round, with normalizing STMs, which of the following tumors is most likely the diagnosis?
expl: Worsening compression on chemotherapy while markers normalize = growing teratoma syndrome, which complicates non-seminomatous germ cell tumours (mixed with teratoma).

why.B: Seminoma responds and any residual mass is necrosis.
why.C: Thymoma isn't treated first with chemo and has no markers.

stem: A pt Presenting with headache and weakness of the arms, later on CT scan shows a posterior mediastinal mass. and asks about the next step ?
expl: A posterior mediastinal mass is usually neurogenic; with neurological symptoms you must exclude intraspinal ("dumbbell") extension → MRI of the spine before any surgery.

why.C: CT already shows the mass; MRI shows the spinal canal.

stem: 45-year-old black African present with SOB and splenomegaly, ct scan show multiple lymphadenopathy around bronchial tree what is dx?
srcNote: One or more answer choices are blank in the source.
expl: Bilateral hilar/peribronchial lymphadenopathy in a Black African patient (with splenomegaly) → sarcoidosis (middle compartment).

why.B: Lymphoma is classically anterior and has B symptoms.
why.C: A cyst doesn't cause multiple nodes and splenomegaly.

stem: A 46-year-old woman came to you complaining of a persistent cough for the past 3 weeks and mild dysphagia. On the exam, she has no respiratory distress. There is an enlarged right lobe of the thyroid gland, without any cervical lymph nodes enlargement. The rest of the examination is unremarkable. Chest X-RAY showed a mass present in the anterior-superior mediastinum displacing the trachea to the left. What could be the next best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: Cough and dysphagia with an enlarged thyroid lobe suggest a retrosternal (substernal) goitre compressing the trachea/oesophagus → CT neck and chest defines the extent and guides the approach.

stem: A woman presented with ptosis, diplopia and lethargy and was diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. She was discovered to have anterior mediastinal mass 6.5*7 consistent with Thymoma. What’s the surgical approach?
expl: Keyed VATS thymectomy: thymoma with MG needs complete thymectomy; minimally invasive (VATS/robotic) thymectomy is now widely used. Very large or invasive thymomas may still need a sternotomy.

why.A: Transcervical access is limited for a 7-cm thymoma.
why.C: Chemo is neoadjuvant for unresectable/advanced thymoma only.

stem: A 25-year-old asymptomatic man incidentally discovered, isolated, rounded, left paravertebral mass on the chest x-ray at the level of T12. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A rounded paravertebral mass in the posterior mediastinum in an asymptomatic young adult = a neurogenic (nerve-sheath) tumour such as a neurofibroma or schwannoma.

why.A: Bronchogenic cysts are middle mediastinal (near the carina).
why.B: Pericardial cysts are at the cardiophrenic angle.

stem: A 23-year-old man had an 8-week history of fever and night sweats accompanied by an 8kg weight loss. The CT scans of the chest shows a heterogeneous mass measuring 6 cm × 8 cm, in the anterior mediastinum. Histological examination shows Reed-Sternberg cells after CT guided needle biopsy. Which one of the following is the best treatment option for this patient?
expl: Reed-Sternberg cells = Hodgkin lymphoma. Lymphoma is treated with chemotherapy (± radiotherapy), not surgery — surgery's role is only biopsy.

why.C: Not the primary treatment and surgery has no role.

stem: A 35-year-old woman was referred to you by her family physician because her chest x-rays showed a mass in the right superior mediastinum. Physical exam shows no palpable masses in the neck or supraclavicular area. CT demonstrates a homogenous, cystic right superior mediastinal mass measuring 5 cmx 4 cm, adjacent to the trachea,There are no other lung nodules or infiltrates. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
expl: A homogeneous cystic mass next to the trachea in the superior/middle mediastinum = bronchogenic cyst (foregut cyst) → excision.

why.A: Pericardial cysts sit at the cardiophrenic angle.
why.C: Cystic hygroma is a cervical lymphatic malformation of children.

stem: Patient had a Mass in his anterior mediastinum. How would you reach the mass to take a biopsy?
srcNote: (Mediastinal pathology) dr note: Anterior do CT guided; Middle to endoscopic
expl: Anterior mediastinal masses are biopsied by CT-guided core biopsy (or anterior mediastinotomy/VATS); cervical mediastinoscopy reaches the middle (paratracheal/subcarinal) nodes, not the anterior compartment.

why.D: Bronchoscopy samples the airway, not the anterior mediastinum.
